expectedText:
ANATOMICAL GIFT (ORGAN AND TISSUE DONATION) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee

DECLARATION OF ANATOMICAL GIFT
I, Jordan Lee, being an adult of sound mind, make this anatomical gift under California Health & Safety Code § 7150.20, to take effect upon my death, for the purpose(s) checked below:

☐ Transplantation ☐ Therapy ☐ Research ☐ Education

This gift is of (check one):
☐ My entire body
☐ The following specific organ(s), tissue(s), or part(s) only: _________________________

Restrictions or limitations on this gift, if any: _________________________

This declaration revokes any earlier document of gift I have made under Health & Safety Code § 7150.20 covering the same organs, tissues, or parts, to the extent inconsistent with it.

WHO MAY MAKE AN ANATOMICAL GIFT OF THEIR OWN BODY
California Health & Safety Code § 7150.15 lets an anatomical gift of a donor's own body or part be made, during the donor's life, for the purpose of transplantation, therapy, research, or education, by: the donor, if the donor is an adult; the donor, if the donor is a minor, but only if the minor is an emancipated minor, or is between 15 and 18 years of age and has the written consent of a parent or guardian; or an agent of the donor, provided the power of attorney for health care or other record expressly permits the agent to make an anatomical gift. Health & Safety Code § 7150.10(a) defines an “adult” as an individual at least 18 years of age, and a “minor” as an individual under 18. The statute conditions eligibility to act on one's own behalf on age, emancipation status, and (for a minor between 15 and 18) parental or guardian consent — its text does not separately state a “sound mind” or other mental-capacity standard for an adult donor acting for themselves.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Subject to Section 7150.35, an anatomical gift of a donor’s body or part may be made during the life of the donor for the purpose of transplantation, therapy, research, or education in the manner provided in Section 7150.20 by any of the following individuals:(a) The donor, if the donor is an adult or if the donor is a minor and is either of the following:(1) An emancipated minor.(2) Between 15 and 18 years of age, only upon the written consent of a parent or guardian.(b) An agent of the donor, provided that the power of attorney for health care or other record expressly permits the agent to make an anatomical gift."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.15, who may make an anatomical gift of one's own body during life (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.15.)
  "(1) “Adult” means an individual who is at least 18 years of age."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.10(a)(1), definition of “adult” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.10.)
  "(15) “Minor” means an individual who is under 18 years of age."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.10(a)(15), definition of “minor” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.10.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's rule for who may make an anatomical gift of their own body — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person, or that other states use the same age thresholds or consent mechanics for minors; some states set different ages or procedures. § 7150.15 (who may act) and § 7150.10 (the chapter's definitions of “adult” and “minor”) are treated here as effectively one source rather than independent ones: § 7150.10 supplies only the defined terms that § 7150.15 uses, not a separate substantive eligibility rule.

HOW AN ANATOMICAL GIFT OF ONE'S OWN BODY CAN BE MADE
California Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(a) lists the ways a donor may make an anatomical gift: by authorizing a statement or symbol indicating the gift to be imprinted on the donor's driver's license or identification card and included on a donor database registry; directly through the Donate Life California Organ and Tissue Donor Registry internet website; in a will; during a terminal illness or injury, by any form of communication that clearly expresses the donor's wish, addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing by the witnesses; or by a donor card or other signed record under subdivision (b). Under subdivision (b), if the donor is physically unable to sign that record personally, another individual may sign it at the donor's direction, but the signing must then be witnessed by at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, and the record must state that it was signed and witnessed in that manner. Revocation, suspension, expiration, or cancellation of a driver's license or identification card on which a gift is indicated does not by itself invalidate the gift, and a gift made by will takes effect at death regardless of whether the will is ever probated or is later invalidated.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A donor may make an anatomical gift through any of the following:(1) By authorizing a statement or symbol indicating that the donor has made an anatomical gift to be imprinted on the donor’s driver’s license or identification card and included on a donor database registry.(2) Directly through the Donate Life California Organ and Tissue Donor Registry Internet Web site.(3) In a will.(4) During a terminal illness or injury of the donor, by any form of communication that clearly expresses the donor’s wish, addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness. The witnesses shall memorialize this communication in a writing and sign and date the writing.(5) As provided in subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(a), the five listed methods of making a gift (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.20.)
  "(b) A donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15 may make a gift by a donor card or other record signed by the donor or other person making the gift or by authorizing that a statement or symbol, indicating that the donor has made an anatomical gift, be included on a donor registry. If the donor or other person is physically unable to sign a record, the record may be signed by another individual at the direction of the donor or other person and shall comply with all of the following:(1) Be witnessed by at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, who have signed at the request of the donor or the other person.(2) State that it has been signed and witnessed as provided in paragraph (1)."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(b), donor card/signed record, and witnessing when signed by another at the donor's direction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.20.)
  "(c) Revocation, suspension, expiration, or cancellation of a driver’s license or identification card upon which an anatomical gift is indicated does not invalidate the gift.(d) An anatomical gift made by will takes effect upon the donor’s death whether or not the will is probated. Invalidation of the will after the donor’s death does not invalidate the gift."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(c)-(d), license/ID changes don't invalidate the gift; a will-based gift takes effect regardless of probate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.20.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's specific list of methods for making an anatomical gift of one's own body — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person, or that other states recognize the same methods; some states, for example, do not treat a driver's license notation alone as sufficient without separate registry enrollment. § 7150.20(a) and § 7150.20(b)-(d) are subsections of the same statutory section, not independent sources, so they are disclosed here as a single source.

HOW AN ANATOMICAL GIFT CAN BE AMENDED OR REVOKED BY THE DONOR
California Health & Safety Code § 7150.25 lets a donor (or other person authorized under § 7150.15) amend or revoke an anatomical gift by: a record signed by the donor, the other authorized person, or — subject to a witnessing requirement — someone signing at that person's direction because they are physically unable to sign, recorded in a donor registry database; or a later-executed document of gift that amends or revokes the earlier gift, either expressly or by inconsistency. A donor may also revoke a gift by destroying the document of gift, or by canceling it on a donor database registry, with the intent to revoke it. A donor may amend or revoke a gift that was not made in a will by any form of communication during a terminal illness or injury addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing. A donor who made the gift in a will may amend or revoke it in the manner used for amending or revoking wills generally, or by the methods described above. Separately, Health & Safety Code § 7150.35(b) clarifies that a donor's own revocation of their gift is not treated as a refusal, and does not by itself bar another authorized person from later making an anatomical gift of the same body or part.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Subject to Section 7150.35, a donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15 may amend or revoke an anatomical gift by either of the following:(1) A record signed by any of the following and recorded in a donor registry database:(A) The donor.(B) The other person.(C) Subject to subdivision (b), another individual acting at the direction of the donor or of the other person, if the donor or other person is physically unable to sign.(2) A later-executed document of gift that amends or revokes a previous anatomical gift or portion of an anatomical gift, either expressly or by inconsistency.(b) A record signed pursuant to subparagraph (C) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) shall comply with all of the following:(1) It shall be witnessed by at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, who have signed at the request of the donor or the other person.(2) It shall state that it has been signed and witnessed as provided in paragraph (1).(c) Subject to Section 7150.35, a donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15 may revoke an anatomical gift by the destruction of the document of gift or cancellation of the document of gift on a donor database registry, or the portion of the document of gift used to make the gift, with the intent to revoke the gift.(d) A donor may amend or revoke an anatomical gift that was not made in a will by any form of communication during a terminal illness or injury addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness. The witnesses shall memorialize this communication in a writing and sign and date the writing.(e) A donor who makes an anatomical gift in a will may amend or revoke the gift in the manner provided for amendment or revocation of wills or as provided in subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.25, the donor's own methods of amending or revoking a gift (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.25.)
  "(b) A donor’s revocation of an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25 is not a refusal and does not bar another person specified in Section 7150.15 or 7150.40 from making an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.20 or 7150.45."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.35(b), a donor's revocation is not a refusal and does not by itself bar others (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.35.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's revocation mechanics for an anatomical gift made by the donor — not a claim about which state's law governs, or that other states offer the same range of revocation methods. The first citation below draws on subdivisions (a) through (e) of a single statutory section (§ 7150.25); the second citation is subdivision (b) of a genuinely different section (§ 7150.35), so the two citations are one source (§ 7150.25) plus one independent source (§ 7150.35(b)), not two fully independent sources.

PRIORITY ORDER TO MAKE A GIFT ON BEHALF OF SOMEONE WHO DID NOT MAKE ONE
Unless barred by a refusal under § 7150.30 or by the preclusive-effect rules of § 7150.35, California Health & Safety Code § 7150.40(a) lets an anatomical gift of a decedent's body or part be made, for transplantation, therapy, research, or education, by any reasonably available member of the following classes, in this order of priority: (1) an agent of the decedent who could have made the gift under § 7150.15(b) immediately before death; (2) the decedent's spouse or domestic partner; (3) the decedent's adult children; (4) the decedent's parents; (5) the decedent's adult siblings; (6) the decedent's adult grandchildren; (7) the decedent's grandparents; (8) an adult who exhibited special care and concern for the decedent during the decedent's lifetime; (9) the persons acting as guardian or conservator of the decedent's person at the time of death; and (10) any other person with authority to dispose of the decedent's body — including a coroner, medical examiner, or hospital administrator — but only after a reasonable effort (deemed satisfied by at least a 12-hour search, with a narrow exception) has been made to locate and inform the higher-priority persons listed. If more than one member of most of these classes is reasonably available, any one of them may make the gift unless that member (or the person the gift would pass to) knows of an objection from another member of the same class, in which case a majority of the reasonably available members must agree. A person may not make the gift if a person in a higher-priority class is reasonably available to make it or to object to it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Subject to subdivisions (b) and (c), and unless barred by Section 7150.30 or 7150.35, an anatomical gift of a decedent’s body or part for the purpose of transplantation, therapy, research, or education may be made by any member of the following classes of persons who is reasonably available, in the following order of priority:(1) An agent of the decedent at the time of death who could have made an anatomical gift under subdivision (b) of Section 7150.15 immediately before the decedent’s death.(2) The spouse or domestic partner of the decedent.(3) Adult children of the decedent.(4) Parents of the decedent.(5) Adult siblings of the decedent.(6) Adult grandchildren of the decedent.(7) Grandparents of the decedent.(8) An adult who exhibited special care and concern for the decedent during the decedent’s lifetime.(9) The persons who were acting as the guardians or conservators of the person of the decedent at the time of death.(10) (A) Any other person having the authority to dispose of the decedent’s body, including, but not limited to, a coroner, medical examiner, or hospital administrator, provided that reasonable effort has been made to locate and inform persons listed in paragraphs (1) to (9), inclusive, of their option to make, or object to making, an anatomical gift.(B) Except in the case where the useful life of the part does not permit, a reasonable effort shall be deemed to have been made when a search for the persons has been underway for at least 12 hours. The search shall include a check of local police missing persons records, examination of personal effects, and the questioning of any persons visiting the decedent before his or her death or in the hospital, accompanying the decedent’s body, or reporting the death, in order to obtain information that might lead to the location of any persons listed."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.40(a), the ten-class statutory priority list (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.40.)
  "(b) If there is more than one member of a class listed in paragraph (1), (3), (4), (5), (6), (7), or (9) of subdivision (a) entitled to make an anatomical gift, an anatomical gift may be made by a member of the class unless that member or a person to which the gift may pass under Section 7150.50 knows of an objection by another member of the class. If an objection is known, the gift may be made only by a majority of the members of the class who are reasonably available.(c) A person shall not make an anatomical gift if, at the time of the decedent’s death, a person in a prior class under subdivision (a) is reasonably available to make, or to object to the making of, an anatomical gift."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.40(b)-(c), majority rule within a class, and the higher-priority-bars-lower rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.40.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's default priority scheme for who may make an anatomical gift on behalf of someone who did not make one themselves — not a claim about which state's law governs, or that other states order priority the same way. This list is governed by a different statute than, and is not identical to, the priority list this corpus's Disposition of Remains Instructions document cites under Health & Safety Code § 7100(a) for who controls burial/cremation decisions; the two statutes were checked independently here rather than assumed to match. Concrete differences found: this anatomical-gift list expressly names ‘the spouse or domestic partner’ at position (2), while the remains-disposition list's statutory text names only a ‘competent surviving spouse’ with no mention of a domestic partner; this list also includes two classes with no counterpart in the remains list — adult grandchildren (6) and grandparents (7) — and ‘an adult who exhibited special care and concern for the decedent’ (8), which the remains list does not have at all; and where the remains list separately names a conservator of the person and a conservator of the estate as two distinct classes, this list combines only ‘guardians or conservators of the person’ into a single class (9), has no counterpart for a conservator of the estate, and instead ends in a residual class (10) for any other person with authority over the body (coroner, medical examiner, hospital administrator) after a documented search. All quoted text in this clause is drawn from subdivisions (a) through (c) of a single statutory section (§ 7150.40); no additional independent source was found for this specific list.

HOW AN ANATOMICAL GIFT INTERACTS WITH AN ADVANCE HEALTH CARE DIRECTIVE
An anatomical gift can be made through an Advance Health Care Directive itself, not only through a separate donor-registry enrollment, license designation, or will: California's optional statutory Advance Health Care Directive form, set out in Probate Code § 4701, states that the form “lets you do either or both of these things. It also lets you express your wishes regarding donation of organs and the designation of your primary physician,” and includes an optional Part 3 letting the person completing it state, “Upon my death, I give my organs, tissues, and parts,” for one or more of transplant, therapy, research, or education purposes. The same statutory form's Part 1 separately gives the named health care agent postdeath authority: “My agent is authorized to donate my organs, tissues, and parts, authorize an autopsy, and direct disposition of my remains, except as I state here or in Part 3 of this form” — meaning an agent's default authority under an Advance Health Care Directive already reaches organ and tissue donation unless the directive limits it. Separately, Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 addresses a possible conflict between an Advance Health Care Directive (or an end-of-life declaration) and a potential anatomical gift over the medical measures needed to keep a part suitable for transplantation or therapy: if the directive's terms conflict with what the gift requires, the prospective donor's attending physician and the prospective donor confer to resolve it; if the prospective donor is incapable of resolving it, the directive's agent (or, absent one or if the agent is not reasonably available, another person otherwise authorized by law to make health care decisions for the prospective donor) acts to resolve it, as expeditiously as possible, and the measures are not withheld or withdrawn before resolution unless doing so is not contraindicated by appropriate end-of-life care.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This form lets you do either or both of these things. It also lets you express your wishes regarding donation of organs and the designation of your primary physician."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4701 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory form's own explanation that it covers organ donation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4701.)
  "PART 3 DONATION OF ORGANS, TISSUES, AND PARTS AT DEATH(OPTIONAL)(3.1)  ◻ Upon my death, I give my organs, tissues, and parts (mark box to indicate yes)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4701, Part 3 (California Legislative Information text), the form's optional organ/tissue/part donation section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4701.)
  "(1.5) AGENT’S POSTDEATH AUTHORITY: My agent is authorized to donate my organs, tissues, and parts, authorize an autopsy, and direct disposition of my remains, except as I state here or in Part 3 of this form:"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4701, Part 1, § 1.5 (California Legislative Information text), the agent's default postdeath donation authority under the form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4701.)
  "(b) If a prospective donor has a declaration or advance health care directive and the terms of the declaration or directive and the express or implied terms of a potential anatomical gift are in conflict with regard to the administration of measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of a part for transplantation or therapy, the prospective donor’s attending physician and prospective donor shall confer to resolve the conflict. If the prospective donor is incapable of resolving the conflict, an agent acting under the prospective donor’s declaration or directive, or, if none, or the agent is not reasonably available, another person authorized by law other than this chapter to make health care decisions on behalf of the prospective donor, shall act for the donor to resolve the conflict. The conflict shall be resolved as expeditiously as possible. Information relevant to the resolution of the conflict may be obtained from the appropriate procurement organization and any other person authorized to make an anatomical gift for the prospective donor under Section 7150.40. Before resolution of the conflict, measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of the part shall not be withheld or withdrawn from the prospective donor if withholding or withdrawing the measures is not contraindicated by appropriate end-of-life care."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7151.10(b), resolving a conflict between a directive/declaration and a potential gift (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7151.10.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two genuinely independent statutory sources from two different California codes: Probate Code § 4701 (the AHCD statutory form, confirming a gift can be made within an Advance Health Care Directive and describing the agent's default postdeath donation authority) and Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 (the anatomical-gift chapter's own conflict-resolution rule for when a directive's terms and a potential gift's needs collide). The three quotes drawn from § 4701 are the same statutory section, not independent of one another, but they are independent of the Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 citation. This is not a claim that using the statutory form is required — Probate Code § 4700, already cited elsewhere in this corpus's Advance Health Care Directive document, states that using it is optional — only that the form the statute itself sets out treats organ donation as something an Advance Health Care Directive can cover. § 7151.10's conflict-resolution rule is narrower than it may first appear: by its own terms it applies specifically to a conflict over ‘measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of a part for transplantation or therapy’ — not to every possible interaction between a directive and a gift.

DOCUMENTING A REFUSAL TO MAKE AN ANATOMICAL GIFT, AND ITS BINDING EFFECT
Separately from making a gift, California Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(a) lets a person refuse to make an anatomical gift of their own body or part by: a record signed by the person (or, subject to a witnessing requirement, signed by someone else at the person's direction if the person is physically unable to sign); the person's will, whether or not it is ever admitted to probate or is later invalidated; or, during the person's terminal illness or injury, any form of communication that clearly expresses the refusal, addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing. A refusal, once made, can itself be amended or revoked: in the same manner used to make a refusal, by later making an anatomical gift under § 7150.20 that is inconsistent with the refusal, or by destroying or canceling the record of refusal with the intent to revoke it. On binding effect, § 7150.30(d) states that, absent an express, contrary statement by the person within the refusal itself, an unrevoked refusal “bars all other persons from making an anatomical gift of the individual's body or part” after that person's death — meaning none of the priority-order decision-makers described elsewhere in this chapter can override it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) An individual may refuse to make an anatomical gift of the individual’s body or part by any of the following:(1) A record signed by either of the following:(A) The individual.(B) Subject to subdivision (b), another individual acting at the direction of the individual if the individual is physically unable to sign.(2) The individual’s will, whether or not the will is admitted to probate or invalidated after the individual’s death.(3) Any form of communication made by the individual during the individual’s terminal illness or injury addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness. The witnesses shall memorialize this communication in a writing and sign and date the writing."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(a), how a refusal to make a gift can be made (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.30.)
  "(c) An individual who has made a refusal may amend or revoke the refusal by any of the following:(1) In the manner provided in subdivision (a) for making a refusal.(2) By subsequently making an anatomical gift pursuant to Section 7150.20 that is inconsistent with the refusal.(3) By destroying or canceling the record evidencing the refusal, or the portion of the record used to make the refusal, with the intent to revoke the refusal."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(c), how a refusal can itself be amended or revoked (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.30.)
  "(d) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (h) of Section 7150.35, in the absence of an express, contrary indication by the individual set forth in the refusal, an individual’s unrevoked refusal to make an anatomical gift of the individual’s body or part bars all other persons from making an anatomical gift of the individual’s body or part."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(d), an unrevoked refusal bars all other persons from making a gift (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.30.)
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (g) and subject to subdivision (f), in the absence of an express, contrary indication by the donor, a person other than the donor is barred from making, amending, or revoking an anatomical gift of a donor’s body or part if the donor made an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.20 or an amendment to an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25.(b) A donor’s revocation of an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25 is not a refusal and does not bar another person specified in Section 7150.15 or 7150.40 from making an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.20 or 7150.45.(c) If a person other than the donor makes an unrevoked anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.20 or an amendment to an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25, another person may not make, amend, or revoke the gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.45.(d) A revocation of an anatomical gift of a donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25 by a person other than the donor does not bar another person from making an anatomical gift of the body or part under Section 7150.20 or 7150.45.(e) In the absence of an express, contrary indication by the donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15, an anatomical gift of a part is neither a refusal to give another part nor a limitation on the making of an anatomical gift of another part at a later time by the donor or another person.(f) In the absence of an express, contrary indication by the donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15, an anatomical gift of a part for one or more of the purposes set forth in Section 7150.15 is not a limitation on the making of an anatomical gift of the part for any of the other purposes by the donor or any other person under Section 7150.20 or 7150.45.(g) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), an individual who is between 15 and 18 years of age may make an anatomical gift for any purpose authorized in this chapter, may limit an anatomical gift to one or more of those purposes, may refuse to make an anatomical gift, or may amend or revoke an anatomical gift, only upon the written consent of the parent or guardian. If a donor who is an unemancipated minor dies, a parent of the donor who is reasonably available may revoke or amend an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part."
  — Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.35 (full text, subdivisions (a)-(g)), the cross-referenced section, as currently published, contains no subdivision (h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=7150.35.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence that a refusal is a real, separately documented act under this chapter, with real binding force on others after death — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person, or that every state gives a refusal the same binding effect. The first two citations below are subdivisions (a) and (c) of a single statutory section (§ 7150.30); no additional independent source was found for those specific points. A verified, notable finding on the third citation: § 7150.30(d)'s binding-effect rule states it applies “Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (h) of Section 7150.35” — but the current text of § 7150.35, fetched and independently re-verified in full (the fourth citation below), contains only subdivisions (a) through (g); no subdivision (h) exists in it as currently published. This cross-reference in the current statutory text could not be resolved from the statute's own language, and is reported here honestly rather than silently corrected or omitted.

SIGNATURE AND WITNESSES
Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

California Health & Safety Code § 7150.20 does not require this declaration to be witnessed or notarized when Jordan Lee signs it personally.

Complete this section only if Jordan Lee is physically unable to sign, so that another individual signs this document at Jordan Lee's direction: the signing must then be witnessed by at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness (someone other than Jordan Lee's spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandchild, grandparent, or guardian, and other than a person to whom the gift could pass), and this document must state that it was signed and witnessed in that manner.

Signature of person signing at Jordan Lee's direction: _________________________ Date: _______________

Witness 1 (disinterested): _________________________ Date: _______________

Witness 2: _________________________ Date: _______________

Statement: This document has been signed and witnessed as required by California Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(b).

—
Groundtruth v1 demo · every "Verified" citation links to a real, checked source.

I, Jordan Lee, being an adult of sound mind, make this anatomical gift under California Health & Safety Code § 7150.20, to take effect upon my death, for the purpose(s) checked below:

☐ Transplantation ☐ Therapy ☐ Research ☐ Education

This gift is of (check one):
☐ My entire body

This declaration revokes any earlier document of gift I have made under Health & Safety Code § 7150.20 covering the same organs, tissues, or parts, to the extent inconsistent with it.

California Health & Safety Code § 7150.15 lets an anatomical gift of a donor's own body or part be made, during the donor's life, for the purpose of transplantation, therapy, research, or education, by: the donor, if the donor is an adult; the donor, if the donor is a minor, but only if the minor is an emancipated minor, or is between 15 and 18 years of age and has the written consent of a parent or guardian; or an agent of the donor, provided the power of attorney for health care or other record expressly permits the agent to make an anatomical gift. Health & Safety Code § 7150.10(a) defines an “adult” as an individual at least 18 years of age, and a “minor” as an individual under 18. The statute conditions eligibility to act on one's own behalf on age, emancipation status, and (for a minor between 15 and 18) parental or guardian consent — its text does not separately state a “sound mind” or other mental-capacity standard for an adult donor acting for themselves.

expectedJSON.body: California Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(a) lists the ways a donor may make an anatomical gift: by authorizing a statement or symbol indicating the gift to be imprinted on the donor's driver's license or identification card and included on a donor database registry; directly through the Donate Life California Organ and Tissue Donor Registry internet website; in a will; during a terminal illness or injury, by any form of communication that clearly expresses the donor's wish, addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing by the witnesses; or by a donor card or other signed record under subdivision (b). Under subdivision (b), if the donor is physically unable to sign that record personally, another individual may sign it at the donor's direction, but the signing must then be witnessed by at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, and the record must state that it was signed and witnessed in that manner. Revocation, suspension, expiration, or cancellation of a driver's license or identification card on which a gift is indicated does not by itself invalidate the gift, and a gift made by will takes effect at death regardless of whether the will is ever probated or is later invalidated.

expectedJSON.body: California Health & Safety Code § 7150.25 lets a donor (or other person authorized under § 7150.15) amend or revoke an anatomical gift by: a record signed by the donor, the other authorized person, or — subject to a witnessing requirement — someone signing at that person's direction because they are physically unable to sign, recorded in a donor registry database; or a later-executed document of gift that amends or revokes the earlier gift, either expressly or by inconsistency. A donor may also revoke a gift by destroying the document of gift, or by canceling it on a donor database registry, with the intent to revoke it. A donor may amend or revoke a gift that was not made in a will by any form of communication during a terminal illness or injury addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing. A donor who made the gift in a will may amend or revoke it in the manner used for amending or revoking wills generally, or by the methods described above. Separately, Health & Safety Code § 7150.35(b) clarifies that a donor's own revocation of their gift is not treated as a refusal, and does not by itself bar another authorized person from later making an anatomical gift of the same body or part.

expectedJSON.body: Unless barred by a refusal under § 7150.30 or by the preclusive-effect rules of § 7150.35, California Health & Safety Code § 7150.40(a) lets an anatomical gift of a decedent's body or part be made, for transplantation, therapy, research, or education, by any reasonably available member of the following classes, in this order of priority: (1) an agent of the decedent who could have made the gift under § 7150.15(b) immediately before death; (2) the decedent's spouse or domestic partner; (3) the decedent's adult children; (4) the decedent's parents; (5) the decedent's adult siblings; (6) the decedent's adult grandchildren; (7) the decedent's grandparents; (8) an adult who exhibited special care and concern for the decedent during the decedent's lifetime; (9) the persons acting as guardian or conservator of the decedent's person at the time of death; and (10) any other person with authority to dispose of the decedent's body — including a coroner, medical examiner, or hospital administrator — but only after a reasonable effort (deemed satisfied by at least a 12-hour search, with a narrow exception) has been made to locate and inform the higher-priority persons listed. If more than one member of most of these classes is reasonably available, any one of them may make the gift unless that member (or the person the gift would pass to) knows of an objection from another member of the same class, in which case a majority of the reasonably available members must agree. A person may not make the gift if a person in a higher-priority class is reasonably available to make it or to object to it.

citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivisions (b) and (c), and unless barred by Section 7150.30 or 7150.35, an anatomical gift of a decedent’s body or part for the purpose of transplantation, therapy, research, or education may be made by any member of the following classes of persons who is reasonably available, in the following order of priority:(1) An agent of the decedent at the time of death who could have made an anatomical gift under subdivision (b) of Section 7150.15 immediately before the decedent’s death.(2) The spouse or domestic partner of the decedent.(3) Adult children of the decedent.(4) Parents of the decedent.(5) Adult siblings of the decedent.(6) Adult grandchildren of the decedent.(7) Grandparents of the decedent.(8) An adult who exhibited special care and concern for the decedent during the decedent’s lifetime.(9) The persons who were acting as the guardians or conservators of the person of the decedent at the time of death.(10) (A) Any other person having the authority to dispose of the decedent’s body, including, but not limited to, a coroner, medical examiner, or hospital administrator, provided that reasonable effort has been made to locate and inform persons listed in paragraphs (1) to (9), inclusive, of their option to make, or object to making, an anatomical gift.(B) Except in the case where the useful life of the part does not permit, a reasonable effort shall be deemed to have been made when a search for the persons has been underway for at least 12 hours. The search shall include a check of local police missing persons records, examination of personal effects, and the questioning of any persons visiting the decedent before his or her death or in the hospital, accompanying the decedent’s body, or reporting the death, in order to obtain information that might lead to the location of any persons listed.

This list is governed by a different statute than, and is not identical to, the priority list this corpus's Disposition of Remains Instructions document cites under Health & Safety Code § 7100(a) for who controls burial/cremation decisions; the two statutes were checked independently here rather than assumed to match. expectedJSON.body: An anatomical gift can be made through an Advance Health Care Directive itself, not only through a separate donor-registry enrollment, license designation, or will: California's optional statutory Advance Health Care Directive form, set out in Probate Code § 4701, states that the form “lets you do either or both of these things. It also lets you express your wishes regarding donation of organs and the designation of your primary physician,” and includes an optional Part 3 letting the person completing it state, “Upon my death, I give my organs, tissues, and parts,” for one or more of transplant, therapy, research, or education purposes. The same statutory form's Part 1 separately gives the named health care agent postdeath authority: “My agent is authorized to donate my organs, tissues, and parts, authorize an autopsy, and direct disposition of my remains, except as I state here or in Part 3 of this form” — meaning an agent's default authority under an Advance Health Care Directive already reaches organ and tissue donation unless the directive limits it. Separately, Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 addresses a possible conflict between an Advance Health Care Directive (or an end-of-life declaration) and a potential anatomical gift over the medical measures needed to keep a part suitable for transplantation or therapy: if the directive's terms conflict with what the gift requires, the prospective donor's attending physician and the prospective donor confer to resolve it; if the prospective donor is incapable of resolving it, the directive's agent (or, absent one or if the agent is not reasonably available, another person otherwise authorized by law to make health care decisions for the prospective donor) acts to resolve it, as expeditiously as possible, and the measures are not withheld or withdrawn before resolution unless doing so is not contraindicated by appropriate end-of-life care.

citations.quote: (b) If a prospective donor has a declaration or advance health care directive and the terms of the declaration or directive and the express or implied terms of a potential anatomical gift are in conflict with regard to the administration of measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of a part for transplantation or therapy, the prospective donor’s attending physician and prospective donor shall confer to resolve the conflict. If the prospective donor is incapable of resolving the conflict, an agent acting under the prospective donor’s declaration or directive, or, if none, or the agent is not reasonably available, another person authorized by law other than this chapter to make health care decisions on behalf of the prospective donor, shall act for the donor to resolve the conflict. The conflict shall be resolved as expeditiously as possible. Information relevant to the resolution of the conflict may be obtained from the appropriate procurement organization and any other person authorized to make an anatomical gift for the prospective donor under Section 7150.40. Before resolution of the conflict, measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of the part shall not be withheld or withdrawn from the prospective donor if withholding or withdrawing the measures is not contraindicated by appropriate end-of-life care.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause draws on two genuinely independent statutory sources from two different California codes: Probate Code § 4701 (the AHCD statutory form, confirming a gift can be made within an Advance Health Care Directive and describing the agent's default postdeath donation authority) and Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 (the anatomical-gift chapter's own conflict-resolution rule for when a directive's terms and a potential gift's needs collide). The three quotes drawn from § 4701 are the same statutory section, not independent of one another, but they are independent of the Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 citation. This is not a claim that using the statutory form is required — Probate Code § 4700, already cited elsewhere in this corpus's Advance Health Care Directive document, states that using it is optional — only that the form the statute itself sets out treats organ donation as something an Advance Health Care Directive can cover. § 7151.10's conflict-resolution rule is narrower than it may first appear: by its own terms it applies specifically to a conflict over ‘measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of a part for transplantation or therapy’ — not to every possible interaction between a directive and a gift.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from making a gift, California Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(a) lets a person refuse to make an anatomical gift of their own body or part by: a record signed by the person (or, subject to a witnessing requirement, signed by someone else at the person's direction if the person is physically unable to sign); the person's will, whether or not it is ever admitted to probate or is later invalidated; or, during the person's terminal illness or injury, any form of communication that clearly expresses the refusal, addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing. A refusal, once made, can itself be amended or revoked: in the same manner used to make a refusal, by later making an anatomical gift under § 7150.20 that is inconsistent with the refusal, or by destroying or canceling the record of refusal with the intent to revoke it. On binding effect, § 7150.30(d) states that, absent an express, contrary statement by the person within the refusal itself, an unrevoked refusal “bars all other persons from making an anatomical gift of the individual's body or part” after that person's death — meaning none of the priority-order decision-makers described elsewhere in this chapter can override it.

This cross-reference in the current statutory text could not be resolved from the statute's own language, and is reported here honestly rather than silently corrected or omitted.
